## Part A — Creating Data Frames

```{r part-a}
# Create a data frame called students containing Student_ID, Name, Age, Major, and GPA
Student_ID <- c(101, 102, 103, 104, 105)
Name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eve")
Age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
Major <- c("CS", "DS", "IT", "CS", "DS")
GPA <- c(3.8, 3.5, 3.9, 2.8, 3.6)

students <- data.frame(Student_ID, Name, Age, Major, GPA)
print(students)

```

- Answer 1: In a matrix, every single value inside has to be the exact same data type, but a data frame is way more flexible because each column can hold a different data type. So I can have text for student names, whole numbers for age, and decimals for GPA all in the same table, as long as all the values inside one single column match.

- Answer 2: When I checked what happens with unequal vector lengths, R threw an error saying arguments imply differing number of rows. This happens because R needs all the vectors to be the exact same length so it can form a clean rectangle without missing values hanging off.

---

## Part B — Subsetting Data Frames

```{r part-b}
# Access the Major column using the $ operator
students$Major

# Access the GPA column using double square brackets [[ ]]
students[["GPA"]]

# Subset rows where GPA is greater than or equal to 3.5
students[students$GPA >= 3.5, ]

# Extract the cell in row 3, column "Name"
students[3, "Name"]

```

- Answer 3: Using `students$Major` directly pulls out the raw values as a flat 1D vector. But when I use `students["Major"]` with single square brackets, R keeps it as a mini 1D data frame instead. Single brackets hold onto the tabular data frame shape, while `$` just gives me the vector inside.

- Answer 4: Writing `students$GPA >= 3.5` makes R test every single row and return a list of `TRUE` or `FALSE` answers. When I put that test inside `students[condition, ]`, R goes line by line and keeps only the rows that got a `TRUE`, while dropping the `FALSE` ones.

---

## Part C — Inspecting Data Frame Properties

```{r part-c}
# Inspect the structure of students using str()
str(students)

# Get summary statistics using summary()
summary(students)

# Display dimensions, row count, column count, and column names
dim(students)
nrow(students)
ncol(students)
names(students)

# Display the first 3 rows using head()
head(students, n = 3)

```

- Answer 5: Running `str()` shows me the inside skeleton of my data frame, like the total rows, columns, and the exact data type of every column. On the other hand, `summary()` gives me math stats like the minimum, maximum, mean, and median for numbers, or counts for text columns.

- Answer 6: The `names()` function lists out all the column headers in my data frame. I always run `names(df)` first to double-check the exact spelling and capital letters so I don't get a `NULL` result by accident when using `$`.

---

## Part D — Data Frame Operations: Adding, Removing, Filtering, and Sorting

```{r part-d}
# Add a new column called Status (Passed if GPA >= 3.0, else Failed)
students$Status <- ifelse(students$GPA >= 3.0, "Passed", "Failed")
print(students)

# Filter for CS majors who passed
students[students$Major == "CS" & students$Status == "Passed", ]

# Sort the data frame by GPA in descending order
students_sorted <- students[order(students$GPA, decreasing = TRUE), ]
print(students_sorted)

# Remove the Status column by setting it to NULL
students$Status <- NULL
print(students)

```

- Answer 7: Assigning `NULL` to a column like `students$Status <- NULL` completely wipes that column out of the data frame and shrinks the total column count by one.

- Answer 8: I used a single ampersand `&` because it checks every single row in the data frame one by one to see if both conditions are true. If I used `&&`, R would only check the very first row and ignore all the rest, which breaks the filter.

## Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge

```{r part-e}
# Combine two student data frames using rbind()
class1 <- data.frame(Student_ID = c(201, 202), Name = c("Fay", "Geo"), GPA = c(3.4, 3.9))
class2 <- data.frame(Student_ID = c(203, 204), Name = c("Hal", "Ivy"), GPA = c(3.1, 3.7))

combined_classes <- rbind(class1, class2)
print(combined_classes)

# Sort the combined data frame by GPA descending and compute the overall average GPA
combined_sorted <- combined_classes[order(combined_classes$GPA, decreasing = TRUE), ]
print(combined_sorted)

mean(combined_classes$GPA)

```

- Answer 9: For `rbind()` to work smoothly, both data frames have to share the exact same column names in the exact same order. If a column name is misspelled or missing in one of them, R freaks out and won't combine them.

- Answer 10: I would use `cbind()` if I wanted to add a brand new column (like `Attendance` or `Quiz_Scores`) for my current set of students. But I would use `rbind()` if I got a list of brand new students and needed to stack them at the bottom of my existing table as new rows.

---

## Conclusion

Data frames are my favorite data structure in R because they act like real spreadsheets, letting me combine numbers and text side by side. Learning how to access columns with `$`, filter rows with logical conditions, and stack data with `rbind()` and `cbind()` makes it really easy to manage real-world datasets like student grade sheets or research results.
